S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator every thermal incident involving overheating, thermal runaway, fire, or explosion, including events without injury or property damage, within 5 business days of learning of it. A death, serious injury, or event presenting an imminent risk to the public must be reported within 24 hours.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: A result above a 5% failure rate requires a corrective-action plan and regulator review, but does not automatically prohibit sale; regulators may require further testing or impose restrictions where results indicate an unreasonable safety risk. Before sale, after material design changes, and annually thereafter, manufacturers must submit per-model results ... and make the results available to customers who buy that model. Results need not be disclosed to the general public.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New units placed on the market from 3 years after this standard takes effect must support a secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. ... complete required retrofits within 6 years of the standard taking effect. Where a retrofit is not technically feasible, the manufacturer must notify affected customers and provide an alternative safety measure.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New units placed on the market beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression designed and validated for the unit's intended installation and use. Regulators may approve equivalent protective designs where they provide comparable risk reduction.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using a consistent installed-unit denominator and regulator-verified data, regulators must promptly review the evidence and may require a recall or other corrective action based on incident severity, test results, and available mitigations. Regulators may order a recall sooner when they determine that a model presents an unreasonable safety risk.

document.section_notes: The final S5 converts the 8-per-100,000 level into a regulator review trigger rather than a mandatory recall, with no bounded corrective-action window, which is the most consequential weakening. S2 keeps the 5% figure only as a corrective-action threshold, so above-limit sales never have to stop, and per-model failure rates go to purchasers and regulators but not the public. S3 delays mandatory shut-off on new units to 36 months while allowing a 6-year retrofit window, and S4 sets suppression at 36 months via a validated-equivalent route; S1 is strong, with 24-hour serious reporting and 5-business-day reporting of all thermal events.
